feedback: If a learner skips the sense step, ask: 'Which part of your body noticed first — your eyes, ears, or skin?'
If a learner skips the muscle step, ask: 'Which muscles moved, and who told them to?'
Praise examples that correctly identify a different starting sense: 'Good — this one started with your ears, not your eyes, but the brain still decided.'
activities.intendedInsight: The loop isn't just in a model — it runs in the child's own deliberate actions, through whichever sense started it.
learnerActions: Think of something YOU do: catching a ball, scratching when you feel an itch, turning when someone calls your name, or answering a question.
Act it out with your body.
Trace it aloud: 'What did my senses tell my brain? What did my brain decide? What did my brain tell my muscles?'
Do a second example that starts with a different sense (hearing, touch, sight).
activities.title: Act out your own loop

feedback: If a learner says the brain is 'only for thinking', give a movement or posture example: 'Right now your brain is keeping you upright — that's a job too.'
Affirm the structure–function point: 'The skull is like a helmet that protects the boss of your body.'
activities.intendedInsight: The brain sits protected inside the skull, which keeps this control centre safe — a simple link between structure and function — and it is busy controlling the body even when you aren't thinking hard.
learnerActions: Feel the hard bone of your skull with your hands.
Talk about why the brain — the body's control centre — is kept inside something hard and strong.
Name one job the brain is doing right now that isn't 'thinking hard', such as keeping you sitting upright.
activities.title: Feel the helmet: where the brain sits
